In summary, our research is concerned with
a new mechanism of the photoperiodic regulation of the circadian system and the role of the central clock in photoperiodism.
elucidating the dynamics of adjustment of the circadian system to a change of photoperiod, as well as the mechanisms of photoperiodic adjustment of the central clock and peripheral clocks.
the dynamics of clock gene expression in the suprarchiasmatic nucleus and in the liver following a change of the light/dark cycle from long to short day lengths.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SCN clock and the liver clock adjust to short photoperiod by different mechanisms, and that the SCN clock adjusts to the change of the photic input in an individual manner of each SCN region.
the adjustment of the SCN and liver clocks to a change of photoperiod is a complex process involving different mechanisms in different brain and peripheral clock regions.

the photoperiodic adjustment is a complex process that involves different mechanisms in different parts of the brain and in the periphery, and that these mechanisms are differentially expressed depending on the clock and the tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the central clock is more sensitive to photoperiod than the peripheral clock, and that both clocks are more sensitive to photic stimuli than to melatonin signals, which is consistent with a role of the central clock as the master pacemaker.

the central SCN clock adjusts to a change of photoperiod by advancing the decline of Per1 and Per2 expression, and the peripheral liver clocks adjust by advancing the decline in Per2 and the rise in Rev-erbalpha.

photoperiod change affects the circadian system in the SCN by modulating the degree of synchronicity between the SCN regions, as well as the waveform of each SCN region's clock gene expression rhythm, while the peripheral liver clock is affected by modulating the waveform of the clock gene expression rhythm.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the photoperiodic adjustment of the SCN clock is a complex process, involving the degree of synchronicity among SCN regions as well as different waveforms of clock gene expression in the individual SCN regions.
the central clock in the SCN and peripheral clocks in the liver are not identical in their response to photoperiod changes.
the photoperiodic change of the circadian system is not a simple advance or delay of the circadian clock.
